patient.chief_complaint: Sudden severe headache 5 days ago, 'just a bad migraine,' now mild persistent headache
patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Adams is a 38-year-old woman with frequent migraines who presents to the emergency department referred by her neurologist for evaluation of an unusual headache that occurred 5 days ago. She reports that 5 days ago she had a sudden onset severe headache that she initially attributed to a migraine, rated 9/10, with photophobia and nausea. She used sumatriptan at onset but the headache did not resolve as quickly as her typical migraines, persisting for about 8 hours. She has had mild residual headache since then, which is unusual as her migraines typically resolve within 4-6 hours. Her neurologist was concerned because: 1) the headache was more sudden than her typical migraines (she describes typical migraines as building over 20-30 minutes, whereas this was instantaneous), 2) she had mild neck stiffness for 2 days after the initial event, and 3) the residual headache is not typical for post-migraine. She has no current neck stiffness. CT was not performed 5 days ago as she and her physicians attributed it to migraine. She denies focal weakness, vision changes other than her typical migraine aura, loss of consciousness, or fever. She denies any exertional trigger. She is now presenting because her neurologist specifically asked her to come to the ED for CT and LP.

ct.impression: Normal non-contrast CT head. No acute intracranial abnormality. No hyperdensity in the subarachnoid space. No mass, hemorrhage, or midline shift. Lumbar puncture recommended if clinical suspicion persists.

results.finding: Spectrophotometry is required for all LP in suspected SAH; visual xanthochromia can be missed
Bilirubin peak persists 2-4 weeks after SAH; xanthochromia by spectrophotometry is diagnostic up to 14-21 days
CT sensitivity for SAH: >98% at 6 hours, ~90% at 24 hours, ~50-85% at 5-7 days - LP required for late presentation
LP mandatory when CT is negative in suspected SAH regardless of time from onset

output.summary: CT sensitivity for subarachnoid hemorrhage declines from >98% within 6 hours to approximately 50–85% at 5–7 days. Lumbar puncture with spectrophotometry for bilirubin is the gold standard for late presentations; xanthochromia by spectrophotometry persists for 2–4 weeks. FLAIR MRI has increased sensitivity compared to non-contrast CT for subacute subarachnoid blood (>72 hours). Clinical correlation recommended.

output.impression: Day 5 TCD (estimated from symptom onset): bilateral ACA mean flow velocity borderline elevated (118–122 cm/s, Lindegaard ratio 3.2); bilateral MCA borderline (98–104 cm/s); basilar normal. Findings are consistent with borderline-mild vasospasm. Clinical correlation recommended.

warnings: Residual headache is from SAH, not migraine

key_reasoning_points: CT sensitivity for SAH drops from >98% at 6 hours to approximately 50-85% at 5 days - LP is essential
Spectrophotometry for bilirubin is the gold standard for late SAH diagnosis (persists 2-4 weeks)
Xanthochromia without RBCs at day 5 is classic - RBCs have lysed, bilirubin remains
The sumatriptan non-response and prolonged headache duration (8+ hours) were red flags distinguishing this from typical migraine
Migraine history is a classic red herring - do not let it prevent SAH workup for thunderclap headache
Day 5 from SAH means peak vasospasm risk is approaching (days 7-14) - nimodipine must be started urgently
FLAIR MRI is an alternative to LP for subacute SAH (>72 hours) when LP is contraindicated or inconclusive
